strengths: Novel formulation that directly matches local features between ground and aerial images and lifts only matched keypoints to BEV using monocular depth, avoiding the information loss inherent in prior BEV-transformation approaches.

Elegant scale-aware Procrustes alignment with a full analytical derivation/proof showing the pose estimate is invariant to unknown depth scale, enabling plug-and-play use of both metric and relative (unscaled) depth predictors without retraining.

Strong empirical gains in the most practically important and challenging settings: 26% reduction in mean localization error on KITTI cross-area, and clear improvements over prior interpretable methods (e.g., FG2) under unknown camera orientation on VIGOR.

High interpretability: the method produces explicit, visualizable local correspondences (Figs. 3, 5, 6, 11) rather than an opaque regression, and qualitative analysis convincingly shows semantically meaningful matches (e.g., shadows, streetlights, road markings).

Very thorough supplementary study: robustness to initial depth scale and max-depth threshold, training/testing with only relative depth, runtime/memory analysis, and honest discussion of failure cases and limitations (non-orthorectified aerial imagery breaking the similarity-transform assumption).
Reasonable ablations (top-point-only vs. all-point coordinate assignment; scale-aware vs. orthogonal Procrustes) that support the design choices.
weaknesses: Mixed results relative to baselines: on KITTI same-area and VIGOR same-area/known-orientation, the method is slightly worse than existing state-of-the-art (e.g., FG2), so gains are concentrated in cross-area/unknown-orientation regimes rather than uniformly across settings.

The core idea builds closely on FG2 (the main baseline), differing primarily in avoiding voxel-based dense querying, adding scale-awareness, and handling unknown orientation; the incremental nature relative to this single close prior work somewhat limits perceived novelty.

The method's correctness relies on the aerial-ground point relationship being a similarity transform, which the paper itself acknowledges is violated by non-orthorectified aerial imagery with visible building façades — a fairly consequential assumption that is not quantitatively analyzed (e.g., how often/severely it is violated).

Orientation error is sometimes higher than regression-based baselines on KITTI, and the explanation (implicit road-direction prior exploited by regression baselines) is plausible but not empirically isolated/verified.
RANSAC is used for VIGOR but explicitly not used for KITTI due to no observed benefit, which is a somewhat ad hoc, dataset-specific design choice without deeper analysis of why.

Comparisons are restricted to a relatively narrow set of recent cross-view localization baselines from the same research lineage; no broader comparison to alternative sensor fusion or learning-based localization paradigms, nor statistical significance/variance reporting across runs.

strengths: The core idea of avoiding an explicit ground-to-BEV warping step and instead lifting only matched keypoints to BEV using monocular depth is well-motivated and elegant, avoiding the information loss (ray-directional distortion, height compression) that affects prior BEV-transformation approaches.

The scale-aware Procrustes alignment is a nice practical extension that lets the method operate with either metric or purely relative (scale-ambiguous) monocular depth predictors at inference time without retraining, which is demonstrated empirically (Fig. 7, Tables 2/4/5) to be robust to several orders of magnitude of scale perturbation.

The paper is mathematically careful: it gives a full derivation/proof (main text and Appendix D) that the scale-aware Procrustes recovers the correct scale under an exact similarity-transform assumption, and clearly states the assumptions under which this holds.

Interpretability is a genuine strength — the method produces explicit, visualizable local correspondences (Figs. 3, 5, 6, 8–11) rather than a black-box pose regression, and the qualitative analysis (success/failure cases, semantic matches like sign-to-shadow) is informative.

Fairly thorough empirical analysis: ablations on coordinate-assignment strategy and scale-awareness (Table 3), robustness to initial scale/depth-threshold choices (Table 4, Fig. 7), plug-and-play evaluation with three different relative-depth predictors (Table 2/5), runtime/memory accounting (Appendix F), and an honest limitations section.
Clear and well-organized writing with good figures illustrating the pipeline and results.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is incremental: the overall pipeline (DINOv2 backbone, dual-softmax matching with learnable dustbins, VCE pose loss) is largely inherited from the closest prior work FG² [52], and the scale-aware Procrustes alignment itself is a direct, fairly standard adaptation of Umeyama's classical similarity-transform solution [43] to this setting, rather than a fundamentally new technical contribution.

The empirical gains are inconsistent and in several important settings the method is actually worse than the main baseline FG²: on KITTI same-area the proposed method has higher mean/median localization error and worse orientation error than FG² (Table 1); on VIGOR with known orientation, the method is clearly worse than FG² in both same-area and cross-area localization (e.g., 3.06m vs 1.95m same-area, 3.43m vs 2.41m cross-area). The headline improvement is confined essentially to the cross-area/unknown-orientation regime, which weakens the generality of the claimed 'superior localization performance under challenging conditions' and makes the overall significance of the contribution more marginal than the abstract suggests.

Evaluation is limited to two datasets (KITTI, VIGOR) that are standard in this sub-area but still narrow; no results are shown on additional cross-view localization benchmarks or under other real-world nuisances (e.g., seasonal/lighting changes, non-flat terrain beyond what KITTI/VIGOR already contain), which would be needed to substantiate the 'well-suited for real-world deployment' claim.

The method's core assumption — that the ground-aerial point correspondences form an exact similarity transform — is acknowledged to be violated by non-orthorectified aerial imagery and perspective distortions of building facades (Appendix G), yet the paper does not quantify how much this violates the pose estimate in practice beyond showing a few qualitative failure cases.

The reliance on an externally frozen, pre-trained monocular depth model is a fairly strong dependency; while the paper shows graceful degradation with less accurate relative depth, the overall accuracy ceiling is still fundamentally bounded by the depth predictor's quality, and the paper does not explore sensitivity to depth models explicitly designed/trained for very different domains (e.g., indoor or off-road).

Some additional implementation choices (e.g., manually determined initial scale factor and maximum depth threshold for relative depth models via 'visually inspecting a few examples') introduce ad hoc, dataset-specific tuning that somewhat undercuts the claimed plug-and-play simplicity of the approach.

Comparisons to baselines are restricted to vision-only cross-view localization methods; there is no discussion of how the method would compare against or integrate with learned/robust outlier-rejection schemes beyond RANSAC, nor statistical significance/variance reporting across runs.

strengths: The core idea—directly matching local ground-aerial features and lifting only the matched keypoints to BEV via monocular depth, rather than warping the entire ground image to BEV—is well-motivated and avoids the information loss/distortion issues of prior BEV-transformation methods.

The scale-aware Procrustes alignment is theoretically grounded; the paper provides a clean derivation (and a full appendix proof) showing the pose/scale estimate is invariant to the scale ambiguity inherent in relative depth, which is an elegant and practically useful property.

Strong empirical results on cross-area generalization: a 26% reduction in mean localization error over the previous SOTA (FG²) on KITTI cross-area, and consistently best orientation error on VIGOR, especially in the more realistic unknown-orientation setting.

High interpretability: the method produces explicit, visualizable correspondences from which pose is analytically computed, in contrast to black-box regression baselines; qualitative figures (including interesting cases like shadow-based matching) support this claim.

Plug-and-play compatibility with multiple relative depth predictors at inference time without retraining, with extensive appendix experiments (scale perturbation robustness, varying max-depth thresholds, training/testing with relative-only depth) that substantiate the robustness claims rather than just asserting them.

Thorough and honest treatment of limitations and failure cases (vegetation-occluded scenes, symmetric layouts, non-orthorectified aerial imagery violating the similarity-transform assumption), plus runtime/memory analysis and broader impact discussion.
weaknesses: Mixed results on same-area settings: the method is slightly worse than prior SOTA on KITTI same-area (localization and orientation) and has slightly higher mean localization error than CCVPE on VIGOR same-area, which somewhat tempers the generality of the claimed improvements.
Evaluation is limited to two datasets (KITTI, VIGOR); no experiments on other geographic regions, sensor types, or more diverse aerial imagery sources to test broader generalization.

Some practical hyperparameters (initial scale factor for relative depth, maximum depth threshold) are set by manual visual inspection per dataset; while shown to be fairly robust in the appendix, this still introduces a degree of manual tuning that slightly undercuts the fully automatic/plug-and-play narrative.

The similarity-transform assumption underlying the Procrustes alignment is acknowledged as violated for non-orthorectified aerial images, but the resulting error is not quantified or isolated experimentally (e.g., via controlled synthetic experiments).
Comparisons in the main tables omit some very recent related methods mentioned in the related work/references (e.g., PIDLoc, BEVSplat), which could better contextualize the reported gains.
No variance/multiple-seed reporting, making it harder to assess the statistical significance of the reported improvements, particularly the narrower margins on same-area settings.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated design choice: performing local feature matching directly in the image plane rather than warping into BEV space (as in prior work FG2), avoiding ray-directional distortions and information loss along the height dimension; this is clearly validated by the BEV-variant ablation (Table 12) showing substantial degradation when matching is done in BEV.

The scale-aware Procrustes alignment is elegant, differentiable, and comes with a complete, correct derivation (including the appendix proof) showing that pose and scale can be recovered consistently even when only relative (non-metric) depth is available at inference — a practically useful property for real-world deployment where metric depth models may be unavailable.

Strong interpretability contribution: correspondences directly determine the pose, enabling RANSAC-based outlier detection and visual overlay of the estimated ground layout onto the aerial image, which is demonstrated to correlate well with localization accuracy and even reveals ground-truth labeling errors in the datasets.

State-of-the-art or highly competitive results on KITTI cross-area and same-area (under ±180° noise) and on VIGOR under unknown orientation, particularly notable given that most prior top-performing methods (e.g., FG2) degrade substantially in unknown-orientation settings.

Extensive ablations and robustness studies (number of correspondences, aerial point resolution, image resolution, RANSAC, temperature, relative-depth scale invariance, training with relative depth only, homography-based alternative pose estimator) that thoroughly probe the design space and support the claimed robustness and simplicity of the method.
Demonstrated cross-dataset generalization to CVACT without retraining, plus reported runtime/memory efficiency showing the method is faster and lighter than the main local-matching baseline (FG2).
weaknesses: Performance is not uniformly state-of-the-art: under known orientation on VIGOR and under ±10° noise on KITTI, the method is often clearly worse than FG2 or other baselines (e.g., Table 2 known-orientation results, Table 1 same-area ±10°), and orientation accuracy specifically lags behind SoTA in several settings, since orientation is only implicitly derived from correspondences rather than optimized directly.

The cross-dataset generalization to CVACT (Sec 4.5, Appendix D) is purely qualitative (a handful of visualizations) with no quantitative metrics, since CVACT reportedly lacks precise localization labels; this weakens the generalization claim, which would benefit from at least an approximate quantitative measure or a larger qualitative sample with failure statistics.

RANSAC is omitted on KITTI because it 'did not yield improvements,' but this observation is not analyzed or explained, leaving a puzzling inconsistency with the VIGOR results where RANSAC clearly helps and is emphasized as a core interpretability/robustness feature.

The method's core novelty is somewhat incremental relative to FG2 (Xia & Alahi, 2025): the main conceptual change is moving matching from BEV space to the image plane and adding scale-awareness to Procrustes; while well executed and empirically justified, the overall pipeline (feature matching + depth lifting + Procrustes + VCE/infoNCE supervision) closely follows the prior work's framework.

The paper relies on a frozen DINOv2 backbone and off-the-shelf monocular depth models (Unik3D, DepthAnythingV2), and results are somewhat sensitive to depth model choice/threshold tuning (e.g., manual initial-scale and max-depth-threshold selection for relative depth), which is acknowledged but adds practical fragility not fully resolved by the robustness ablations shown.

Some failure cases (dense vegetation, occlusion by high-rises, repetitive markings) are acknowledged as common challenges rather than limitations of the specific approach, but no quantitative breakdown of failure-mode frequency or their impact on overall metrics is provided, making it harder to judge real-world reliability.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated limitation of prior BEV-based cross-view localization (FG^2): matching directly in the image plane rather than through a distorted BEV warp, avoiding ray-directional distortion and height-dimension information loss.

The scale-aware Procrustes alignment is differentiable, analytically derived (with full proofs in the appendix), and elegantly handles both metric and up-to-scale relative monocular depth, which is a practically useful property for deployment with different depth predictors.

Strong and genuinely useful interpretability: correspondences can be visualized, RANSAC inlier ratio correlates with pose error, and overlaying the re-scaled ground layout on the aerial image provides an intuitive failure/success diagnostic, even revealing ground-truth labeling errors in the datasets.

Extensive ablation studies (number of correspondences, aerial point resolution, temperature, RANSAC, BEV-vs-image-plane matching, homography-vs-Procrustes pose estimation, relative-depth training/inference) substantially support the design choices.
Reasonable generalization results via direct transfer to CVACT without retraining, plus runtime/memory analysis showing the method is lighter and faster than FG^2.
weaknesses: Quantitative results are inconsistent: the method is not uniformly state-of-the-art and in several important settings clearly underperforms competitors (e.g., VIGOR known-orientation mean localization 3.43m vs FG^2's 2.41m; KITTI same-area ±10° mean 1.13m vs FG^2's 0.75m; KITTI cross-area ±180° falls short of SliceMatch). This undercuts the general 'state-of-the-art' framing used in the abstract/intro.

Orientation estimation is notably weaker than competing methods on KITTI, and the paper's explanation (not exploiting the road-alignment prior) is somewhat post-hoc rather than a design feature, suggesting the analytic-pose approach sacrifices accuracy for interpretability in some regimes.

The core technical contribution is incremental relative to FG^2: swapping BEV-plane matching for image-plane matching plus a known closed-form (Umeyama) scale-aware Procrustes solver; the novelty is modest rather than a fundamentally new paradigm.

The interpretability claims, while visually compelling, are largely qualitative (curated example figures) and only lightly quantified (one inlier-ratio-vs-error plot); there is no systematic/quantitative evaluation of how well the correspondence-based interpretability predicts failure compared to alternative uncertainty/confidence estimates from baseline methods.

The 2D similarity (Procrustes) formulation implicitly assumes the aerial image behaves like a true orthophoto (TDOM), which the authors themselves acknowledge is not the case for standard DOMs used in VIGOR/KITTI (building facade distortions); the mitigation discussion in Appendix I is reasonable but remains a model mismatch that is not rigorously quantified in terms of its error contribution.

Baselines compared are mostly prior cross-view localization works; no comparison to more recent generic 3D/2D matching foundation models (e.g., MASt3R, VGGT, mentioned only in passing) that could plausibly be adapted to this task.
Some ablation conclusions (e.g., RANSAC only used on VIGOR, omitted on KITTI 'as it did not yield improvements') suggest brittle or dataset-specific tuning rather than a universally robust pipeline.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated limitation of prior BEV-plane matching work (FG²): warping to BEV introduces ray-directional distortions and loses height information, and the paper clearly demonstrates (Table 12, Fig. 7) that image-plane matching + lifting to BEV outperforms a BEV-plane matching variant with the same backbone/losses.

The scale-aware Procrustes alignment is theoretically grounded, with a full derivation and proof provided in the appendix, and elegantly supports both metric and unknown-scale relative depth within a single differentiable, end-to-end trainable pipeline supervised only by weak camera-pose labels (no pixel-level annotations).

Strong interpretability contribution: correspondences are directly visualizable and quantitatively correlate with pose error (Fig. 4), enable RANSAC-based outlier rejection, and the re-scaled ground layout overlay on aerial imagery provides an intuitive, qualitatively convincing visual diagnostic (including catching ground-truth labeling errors in VIGOR, Fig. 5c).

Extensive empirical validation across two datasets (KITTI, VIGOR) with both same-area/cross-area and known/unknown orientation settings, state-of-the-art or highly competitive results especially in the harder cross-area and unknown-orientation regimes, plus zero-shot cross-dataset generalization to CVACT.

Thorough ablation studies (main paper + large appendix) covering correspondence count, aerial point density, resolution, temperature, RANSAC, training settings, relative-depth robustness, and scale robustness (±3 orders of magnitude initial scale), supporting the claimed robustness and practicality.
Good engineering transparency: runtime/memory comparison against FG², reproducibility statement, and an LLM usage disclosure.
weaknesses: Mixed competitiveness against SOTA: in several known-orientation / same-area settings (VIGOR known orientation, KITTI ±10° same-area) the method is clearly outperformed by FG² and sometimes CCVPE/HC-Net, and orientation accuracy on KITTI is explicitly noted as worse than SOTA since the method cannot exploit the road-alignment prior; the gains are concentrated in the cross-area/unknown-orientation regime, somewhat narrowing the claimed 'state-of-the-art' breadth.

Cross-dataset generalization to CVACT is only evaluated qualitatively (via correspondence/layout visualizations) because CVACT lacks precise localization labels; without any quantitative proxy metric, generalization claims rest on cherry-picked qualitative examples.

The method's accuracy is fundamentally bounded by the quality of off-the-shelf monocular depth predictions, and while robustness to scale is shown, the impact of systematic depth errors (e.g., on thin/overhanging structures, parallax inconsistencies) on correspondence quality is not deeply analyzed beyond a coarse depth-threshold ablation.

The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental relative to FG²: it largely swaps where matching happens (image plane vs. BEV plane) and adds a scale-aware Procrustes solver on top of an otherwise similar pipeline (DINOv2 backbone, dual-softmax matching, VCE/infoNCE losses); the conceptual leap is moderate even though the empirical execution is thorough.

Interpretability is demonstrated mainly through qualitative visualizations and one correlation plot (inlier ratio vs. error); there is no quantitative benchmark or user study establishing the practical value of the 'interpretability' claims relative to other methods.

The assumption of a 3-DoF rigid similarity transform (plus the implicit TDOM-like aerial image assumption discussed in Appendix I) is acknowledged as an approximation; failure cases involving dense vegetation, occlusion by high-rises, and repetitive structures remain significant, and the gap between same-area and cross-area performance (e.g., VIGOR unknown-orientation mean error 2.21m vs 9.54m) is still large.
